title: Selective Etching Quaternary MAX Phase toward Single Atom Copper Immobilized MXene (Ti3C2Clx) for Efficient CO2 Electroreduction to Methanol
abstract: Single atom catalysts possess attractive electrocatalytic activities for various chemical reactions owing to their favorable geometric and electronic structures compared to the bulk counterparts. Herein, we demonstrate an efficient approach to producing single atom copper immobilized MXene for electrocatalytic CO2 reduction to methanol via selective etching of hybrid A layers (Al and Cu) in quaternary MAX phases (Ti3(Al1−xCux)C2) due to the different saturated vapor pressures of Aland Cu-containing products. After selective etching of Al in the hybrid A layers, Cu atoms are wellpreserved and simultaneously immobilized onto the resultant MXene with dominant surface functional group (Clx) on the outmost Ti layers (denoted as Ti3C2Clx) via Cu−O bonds. Consequently, the as-prepared single atom Cu catalyst exhibits a high Faradaic efficiency value of 59.1% to produce CH3OH and shows good electrocatalytic stability. On the basis of synchrotron-based X-ray absorption spectroscopy analysis and density functional theory calculations, the single atom Cu with unsaturated electronic structure (Cu, 0 < δ < 2) delivers a low energy barrier for the rate-determining step (conversion of HCOOH* to absorbed CHO* intermediate), which is responsible for the efficient electrocatalytic CO2 reduction to CH3OH.

sections.text:
Reducing the sizes of metal-based catalysts to nano-particles,1 sub-nanometer clusters,2 or a single atomlevel3−5 is of great significance as the active sites can be largely increased and even maximized. In particular, single atom catalysts (SACs) with uniformly dispersed active metal centers exhibit intrinsic highly unsaturated coordination nature and quantum confinement effect,6,7 leading to a high electron density distribution in the vicinity of the Fermi level, which facilitates fast electron transfer during catalytic reactions.8−11
Such favorable characteristics thus make SACs as ideal electrocatalysts for various reactions in green chemistry including carbon dioxide reduction reaction (CRR),12−14 hydrogen evolution reaction (HER),15 and oxygen evolution reaction (OER).16 For example, single atom nickel on nitrogen-doped graphene exhibits good electrocatalytic activities for CRR, since single atom Ni sites are favorable for the formation of COOH* intermediate with a low binding energy
and simultaneously facilitate the desorption of CO with a low barrier.17
To produce SACs, some approaches including co-precipitation,18 wet impregnation,19 and atomic layer deposition20
have been explored by introducing single atoms onto/into supporting materials, which can be collectively called a bottomup approach. In this manner, various single atom catalysts such as single atom Cu,21 Ni,22 and Co23 have been produced on the basis of transition metal-containing precursors and exhibited high electrocatalytic activities. Despite that all

SACs can be facilely produced via the bottom-up approach, some single atoms are inevitably and congenitally buried in the supporting materials. The unexposed single atoms would lose the catalytic activities owing to the unavailable mass-transfer pathways. To address this issue, one efficient strategy is to preconfine the individual active atoms into a specific region of the layered structures, which are then exfoliated to ultrathin 2D layers to maximally expose the active atoms, called a top-down approach.24,25 In this context, single atom W decorated Ni(OH)2 layers were recently prepared through facilely ultrasonic exfoliation of the W-containing bulk counterpart and showed the reportedly highest OER activities of 80 mA cm−2 at a low overpotential of 267 mV owing to their largely exposed single atom W with abundant outermost vacant orbitals, which are beneficial to the adsorption of OH− and H2O at the exposed single atom W site of Ni(OH)2 layers and formation of the O−O coupling at the same active sites.26 Thus, the top-down approach is becoming an ideal strategy to produce SACs with highly exposed catalytically active sites and high activities for a variety of reactions. It is well-known that MAX phases, with the general formula of Mn+1AXn (n = 1−4), possess a well-defined layer structure, where M is an early transition metal, A is an IIIA/IVA group element, and X is C and/or N.27,28 Moreover, in a regular MAX phase, multielements with an alloying feature can be randomly occupied in the single-atom-thick A layers29,30 and may provide an ideal platform to produce SACs. As a proof of the concept, here, single atom copper immobilized MXene layers are prepared via selective etching of atomic-level hybrid A layers (Al and Cu) from quaternary MAX phases (Ti3(Al1−xCux)C2). The essence of this approach is selectively removing one element by employing the easy sublimation properties of their A-containing product (AlCl3) and leaving the other unreacted A element (Cu) onto MXene with the dominant surface functional group (Clx) on the outmost Ti layers (denoted as Ti3C2Clx). Consequently, the as-prepared single atom Cu catalyst exhibits a high Faradaic efficiency (FE)
value of 59.1% to produce CH3OH and shows good electrocatalytic stability. According to the synchrotron-based X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) and extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) analysis, the single atoms of Cu are coordinated by three O atoms with unsaturated electronic structure (Cuδ+, 0 < δ < 2). Moreover, the DFT calculations reveal that the single atoms of Cu prefer the easier downhill type for the conversion of OCHO* to absorbed HCOOH* intermediate and deliver a low energy barrier for the rate-determining step (conversion of HCOOH* to absorbed CHO* intermediate), benefiting electrocatalytic CO2 reduction to CH3OH.

sections.heading: RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
sections.text:
The synthetic procedures of single atom Cu immobilized MXene were schematically illustrated in Figure 1a. Initially, Cu- and Al-containing quaternary MAX phase, Ti3(Al1−xCux)C2 (x = 0−0.1), was synthesized via ball-milling treatment for 20 h and subsequent sintering at 1400 °C (Supporting Information Figures S1 and S2), similar to Nechiche’s procedures.30 According to the Al−Cu binary phase diagram (Figure 1b), Cu and Al could form a tunable Al1−xCux liquid molten alloy above 1100 °C, ensuring the mutual diffusion of Cu and Al atoms in the single-atom-thick A layers of MAX phase. The X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of the as-prepared Cu- and Al-containing quaternary MAX phase (Figure S1) are well-consistent with the reported Ti3(Al1−xCux)C2.
30,31 Subsequently, the as-prepared quaternary MAX phase was dispersed into molten zinc chloride at 600 °C, where Al layers in MAX phase reacted with zinc chloride to produce AlCl3. Owing to the easy sublimation nature of the byproduct AlCl3, Al atoms in the A layers would be selectively etched away (Figure S3), and the unreacted Cu atoms were well-preserved, generating accordion-like single atom Cu immobilized MXene (Figure 1c,d). After sonication, the accordion-like MXene could be exfoliated to ultrathin single atom Cu immobilized MXene layers, which were denoted as SA-Cu-MXene.
https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acsnano.0c09755 ACS Nano 2021, 15, 4927−4936
4928
Meanwhile, Cu-particles-MXene and MXene were synthesized by the same method. As shown in Figure S4, clearly, all of these samples showed the characteristic peaks of MXenes, suggesting the successful conversion from MAX to MXenes. The microstructure of the obtained SA-Cu-MXene was first analyzed via field emission−scanning electron microscopy (FESEM) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM). As shown in Figure S5, many two-dimensional (2D) layers with lateral sizes of several micrometers are visible. And SEM images of Cu-particles-MXene and MXene samples can be seen in Figures S6 and S7. TEM images further reveal the smooth surfaces of the resultant layers (Figures 2a and S8), and there are no distinct nanoparticles or clusters on the layer surface, which is the same as MXene (Figure S9). In the TEM image of Cu-particles-MXene, there are some particles on the layer surface and the HRTEM image shows an interplanar spacing of 0.13 nm, corresponding to the spacing of (220) planes of Cu (Figure S10). The thickness of the layers is evaluated to be ∼2 nm (Figure 2b) by atomic force microscopy (AFM). Moreover, high-resolution TEM (HRTEM) image discloses an obvious interlayer spacing of 0.26 nm, in good accordance with the reported d(0110) of Ti3C2Tx MXene (Figure S11).
32,33 Selected area electron diffraction (SAED) patterns exhibit only one set of hexagonally arranged diffraction spots, verifying a single-crystalline structure of the MXene layers (inset in Figure S11). The content of Cu in the resultant sample is evaluated to be 1.0 wt % by inductively coupled plasma−atomic emission spectroscopy (ICP-AES). To definitively identify the dispersion states Cu atoms on
MXene layers, aberration-corrected high-angle annular darkfield scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADFSTEM) was carried out. As shown in Figures 2c and S12, a large number of isolated bright dots can be clearly discerned
on the surface of the resultant layers. Then, we conducted an electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS) scan; however, there was no distinct signal from Cu (Figure S13), which was due to the relatively low concentration of Cu single atoms. Note that the absence of Zn signals in EELS and the very low content of Zn (0.1 wt %) detected by the ICP-AES strongly suggested that these white dots were ascribed to the isolated Cu atoms. Moreover, the existence of the Cu single atoms could also be indicated by the EDS mapping (Figure S14). The coordination environment of the copper in SA-Cu-
MXene was further characterized by synchrotron-based X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) and extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS). As shown in Figure 2f, the near-edge absorption energy curve of SA-Cu-MXene is located between the CuO and Cu foil curves, clearly revealing the highly unsaturated electronic structure of Cuδ+ (0 < δ < 2).34,35
The corresponding Fourier transformed EXAFS spectra of the R space for SA-Cu-MXene only show one dominant peak at an approximate distance of 1.54 Å (Figure 2e), which is nearly identical to the peak of CuO reference sample (Cu−O bonds, 1.55 Å) and far from the Cu−Cl bonds (2.39 Å), suggesting the interaction between Cu and O atoms on the surface of MXene.36,37 Moreover, there is few Cu−Cu coordination (2.18 Å) detected, strongly confirming that Cu is in the state of single atom on MXene in contrast with the Cu-particlesMXene samples (Figure S15), in good agreement with above aberration-corrected HAADF-STEM observation. Furthermore, the quantitative EXAFS fitting was conducted to show the detailed atomic structure and the coordination environment of Cu atom on the SA-Cu-MXene assisted with CuO standard sample (Figure S16). The results are showed in Figure 2f, and the fitting parameters are listed in Table S1. The fitting results revealed that the Cu atom on the SA-Cu-MXene was coordinated by three O atoms under the results of the
https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acsnano.0c09755 ACS Nano 2021, 15, 4927−4936
4929
coordination number being 3.2 ± 0.4 with a bond length of 1.92 ± 0.02 Å. Then, as shown in Figure 3a, the X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was conducted to compare the surface compositions and chemical states of SA-CuMXene, Cu-particles-MXene, and MXene. A weak signal of Cu 2p3/2 peak at ∼933.7 eV38,39 can be detected in SA-Cu-MXene compared to Cu-particles-MXene (Figure 3b), indicating a low Cu content. Moreover, the high-resolution O 1s spectra for SA-Cu-MXene can be deconvoluted into three peaks at 530.5, 532.0, and 533.4 eV, corresponding to O−Ti, Ti3C2−Ox, and Ti3C2−OH, respectively (Figure 3c).40,41 The Ti 2p spectra are also deconvoluted to Ti−C, Ti−O, and Ti−Cl bonds at 455.1/460.9, 456.5/461.9, and 459.0/464.5 eV, respectively. (Figure 3d).42
The electrocatalytic properties of SA-Cu-MXene for CRR were tested in a two-compartment electrochemical cell with CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte for 30 min. Clearly, SA-Cu-MXene exhibits much higher current density in the CO2-saturated electrolyte than that in Ar-saturated electrolyte, indicating the high electrocatalytic activities of SA-Cu-MXene toward electrocatalytic CRR (Figure 4a). In the case of SA-CuMXene, a high value of 21.3 mA cm−2 is achieved at −1.4 V (vs RHE in the whole text) in the CO2-saturated electrolyte, which is much higher than those of Cu-particles-MXene (9.6 mA cm−2) and MXene (3.7 mA cm−2) under the same testing conditions (Figure 4b). The CRR selectivity of SA-Cu-MXene was further evaluated at various potentials by chronoamperometry tests, together with nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) and gas chromatography (GC), to analyze the liquid and gas products, respectively. As shown in Figure 4c, a typical volcano-shaped FE (CH3OH) dependence is presented at the applied potentials from −1.1 to −1.8 V. At −1.4 V, a maximum CH3OH FE of 59.1% is achieved (Figure S17), which is significantly higher than that of Cu-particles-MXene (14.6% at −1.4 V) (Figure 4d) and also higher than those recently reported for single atom Cu decorated carbon membranes (44% for CH3OH product)
21 and graphene anchored single atom Cu catalyst (without any CH3OH product). 43 Notably,
SA-Cu-MXene shows highly negative potential for CRR, which may be originated from the poor conductivity (Table S2) that reduces the kinetics of the electrocatalytic process (Figure S18). To understand the effect of Cu contents on the electrocatalytic properties of SA-Cu-MXene for CRR, we synthesized different Cu level SA-Cu-MXene by selectively the etching quaternary MAX phase (Ti3(Al1−xCux)C2) (x = 0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1). As shown in Figure S19, 2% Cu-MXene shows higher CH3OH FE than 1% Cu-MXene and 5% or 10% CuMXene owing to the appropriate single atom loading and monodispersion properties. Meanwhile, we conducted a blank experiment to eliminate the impact of other external factors by using blank Nafion dispersion dropped onto a working electrode for the electrocatalytic test. Clearly, as shown in Figure S20, after catalyzing for 30 min, no any methanol product could be detected by NMR. In contrast, the MXene sample shows negligible electrocatalytic CO2 reduction activity with little CO product throughout all of the applied potentials (Figures 4e and S21). Therefore, the CH3OH product should be catalyzed by the Cu atoms on the surface of MXene layers. More importantly, even after 30 h testing, SA-Cu-MXene still exhibits the stable current density (Figure 4f) and high CH3OH FE of >58%, demonstrating the good stability of the SA-Cu-MXene catalyst for CRR. After electrocatalytic CRR test, the 2D morphology and isolated dispersed Cu atoms of SA-Cu-MXene can be well-maintained (Figure S22). This is in contrast to the easily oxidized MXene-Ti3C2Tx in aqueous dispersions owing to the good protection of the electroreduction environment from −1.0 to −1.8 V. The double-layer capacitances (Cdl) were further calculated to identify the influence of electrochemical active surface areas (ECSAs) for the high activity of SA-Cu-MXene. As illustrated in Figure S23, the Cdl of SA-Cu-MXene is 9.9 mF cm
−2, almost the same as those of Cu-particles-MXene (10.6 mF cm−2) and MXene (9.7 mF cm−2) samples, suggesting that the high activities of SA-Cu-MXene should be attributed to other factors such as single atom Cu sites rather than the high ECSAs. During the testing time for 30 h, the slightly increased
https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acsnano.0c09755 ACS Nano 2021, 15, 4927−4936
4930
current density maybe resulted from the increased real ESCAs of SA-Cu-MXene (Figure S24). As shown in the electrochemical impedance spectra (EIS, Figure S25), SA-Cu-MXene exhibits a small charger-transfer resistance, confirming that the single atom Cu on MXene can significantly promote the electrons transport to the CO2 molecules on the surface of SACu-MXene. Associated with above structural analysis, the high activities of SA-Cu-MXene for electroreduction of CO2 to CH3OH may be originated from the following reason: atomically dispersed Cu sites would greatly inhibit the dimerization (or C−C coupling) of the C1 intermediates (such as *CO) to produce C2+ products (such as C2H5OH), thus facilitating the achievement of a high selectivity to produce CH3OH. 44−47
To gain further insight into the intrinsic property and reactivity of SA-Cu-MXene and Cu-particles-MXene, density functional theory (DFT) calculations were carried out on the basis of the model of EXAFS fitting results. As indicated by the EXFAS fitting results, the model of 3 × 3 single atom copper immobilized MXene functionalized by O atoms supercell with a Cu atom was established and charge density in SA-CuMXene was displayed in Figure 5a; the orange region denotes charge density depletion around a Cu single atom, revealing
that the Cu is positively charged with Cu−O3 structure. Then the as-proposed reaction pathways of CO2 reduction as well as diagram were manifested in Figure 5b,c. According to the DFT calculations, single atom Cu and nanoparticle Cu(100) (Figure S26) on the MXene preferred the pathway of the conversion of CO2* to absorbed OCHO* intermediate rather than COOH* intermediate due to the easier downhill type compared to uphill type in terms of thermodynamics. In the proposed CO2RR pathway, single atom Cu on MXene showed better advantageous free energies (0.15 eV) than nanoparticle Cu (0.27 eV) in the conversion of CO2 to absorbed CO2* molecule. The conversion of HCOOH* to absorbed CHO* molecule is the rate-determining step (RDS)48 for the SA-CuMXene, and the conversion of OCHO* to absorbed HCOOH* intermediate is the RDS for the Cu-particlesMXene. Especially, the conversion of OCHO* to absorbed HCOOH* intermediate is downhill type to the SA-Cu-MXene, and Cu-particles-MXene is an uphill type, which revealed that single atom Cu could significantly reduce the energy barriers toward electrocatalytic CO2 reduction to CH3OH owing to the unsaturated electronic structure of single atom Cu. Also, SACu-MXene shows better advantageous free energies (0.53 eV)
https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acsnano.0c09755 ACS Nano 2021, 15, 4927−4936
4931
for RDS, while Cu-particles-MXene shows higher free energies (0.92 eV) for RDS.

sections.heading: CONCLUSIONS
sections.text:
In conclusion, single atom copper immobilized MXene layers were synthesized via selective etching of atomic-level hybrid A layers (Al and Cu) from quaternary MAX phases (Ti3(Al1−xCux)C2). After selective etching of Al layers, single atom Cu was well-preserved and simultaneously immobilized onto MXene (Ti3C2Clx). Consequently, the as-prepared single atom Cu catalyst exhibits a high Faradaic efficiency value of 59.1% to produce CH3OH and shows good electrocatalytic stability. On the basis of XAS analysis and DFT calculations, the single atoms Cu with unsaturated electronic structure (Cuδ+, 0 < δ < 2) deliver a low energy barrier for the ratedetermine step (conversion of HCOOH* to absorbed CHO* intermediate), which is responsible for the efficient electrocatalytic CO2 reduction to CH3OH. We anticipate that our simple top-down synthetic protocol can be further extended to
produce many SACs with broadened applications based on the big family of quaternary and multielement-containing MAX phases.

sections.heading: EXPERIMENTAL SECTION
sections.text:
Material Synthesis. Synthesis of Quaternary MAX-Ti3(Al1−xCux)C2. Specifically, titanium, aluminum, copper, and graphite powders with a molar ration of 3:(1 − x):x:2 were mixed and followed by ball milling for 20 h, where x = 0−0.1. The as-prepared powders were placed in a tube furnace under flowing Ar and heated to 1400 °C for 4 h at a ramp rate of 10 °C min−1. After cooling to room temperature, the sample was milled to produce Ti3(Al1−xCux)C2 fine powders. Then, homemade Ti3(Al0.98Cu0.02)C2, Ti3(Al0.9Cu0.1)C2, and Ti3AlC2 were used to prepare SA-Cu-MXene, Cu-particles-MXene, and MXene layers, respectively.
Synthesis of SA-Cu-MXene. A 1 g amount of Ti3(Al0.98Cu0.02)C2 and 5 g of ZnCl2 were mixed thoroughly in a mortar under the protection of Ar. After grinding for 1 h, the as-obtained mixture was transferred into an alumina crucible. Then the alumina crucible was heated at 600 °C for 5 h at ramp rate of 5 °C min−1. After that, the product was dispersed in hydrochloric acid (4 M) and the mixture
https://dx.doi.org/10.1021/acsnano.0c09755 ACS Nano 2021, 15, 4927−4936
4932
was stirred for 20 h at room temperature. Then the dispersion was washed for 6 times with argon-saturated water and sonicated for 20 h. Finally, SA-Cu-MXene was obtained after freeze-drying treatment for 48 h. The synthetic procedures of Cu-particles-MXene and MXene were similar to that of SA-Cu-MXene except that Ti3(Al0.9Cu0.1)C2 and Ti3AlC2 were used as the MAX phase precursors, respectively. Materials Characterization. The morphologies and microstructures of the samples were characterized by field emission scanning electron microscopy (JEOL-7500) and high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (JEOL, NEM-2100F). X-ray diffraction (Rigaku D/max2500PC) was carried out using Cu Kα radiation over the range of 5−80°. Chemical states were characterized by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (Thermo Escalab 250Xi). Aberration-corrected high-angle annular dark field−scanning transmission electron microscopy was performed on double aberrationcorrected TEM 0.5 microscopy at 300 kV using a high-angle annular detector, resulting in “Z-contrast” images. Electron energy loss spectroscopy experiment was conducted at an aberration-corrected JEOL ARM 200 microscopy. The energy resolution is about 0.6 eV. The X-ray absorption fine structure (XAFS) spectra were conducted at the 1W1B station of the Beijing Synchrotron Radiation Facility. The storage rings of the Beijing Synchrotron Radiation Facility were carried out at 2.5 GeV with a maximum current of 250 mA. A Veeco/ Bruker (ICON) atomic force microscope was used to characterize the thickness of the sample. The Cu contents in the SA-Cu-MXene were measured by ICP-ASE (Optima-7000DV). The electrical conductivity was tested by a four-point-probe method by a resistivity tester (Suzhou Jingge, China). Analysis of XAFS Data. The experimental data of XAFS were processed in the standard procedures with the ATHENA module implemented in IFEFFIT software packages.49,50 After subtraciting the post-edge background from the overall absortion and normalizing with respect of the edge jump step, the EXAFS spectra were gained. Then the Fourier transformation of χ(k) data in k-space ranging from 2.1 to 10.6 Å−1 was carried out by using Hanning windows (dk = 1.0 Å−1) and the EXAFS contributions was separated from various coordination shells. The quantitative data could be obtained by leastsquares curve fitting in R-space with the Fourier transform k-space range of 2.1 to 10.6 Å−1, with the module ARTEMIS of programs in IFEFFIT. Electrochemical Measurement. All electrochemical experiments were conducted in a typical gastight two-compartment H-type threeelectrode electrochemical cell with cation exchange membrane (Nafion-115, ∼4 cm2) as the compartment separator. A glass carbon electrode coated with catalysts was used in the cathode compartment as a working electrode; the catalysts loading was 0.29 mg cm−2. An Ag/AgCl (KCl-saturated) electrode and a carbon rod electrode were used as the reference and counter electrode, respectively. In a typical preparation procedure of the working electrode, 4 mg of the catalyst and 80 μL of Nafion solution (5 wt %) were dispersed into 0.92 mL of water and ethanol solution with a volume ratio of 4:1. Then, 5 μL of the solution was loaded onto a glass carbon electrode (0.07 cm2) to prepare a working electrode. All electrocatalytic experiments were carried out with a CO2 gas flow rate of 3 sccm to saturated CO2 in the electrolyte. Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) measurement was recorded at a scan rate of 10 mV s−1 in the potential between 0 and −2.0 V vs RHE. The electrolyte in the cathode compartment was stirred during the electrocatalytic reaction of 30 min for each applied potential. Durability tests were performed at −1.4 V vs RHE for 30 h. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy plots were tested with an amplitude of 5 mV in a frequency range from 100 kHz to 0.1 Hz. All potentials were converted to the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) reference scale by the following equation: V(RHE) = V(Ag/AgCl) + 0.197 + 0.059pH. During the reaction, gas phase products were analyzed and quantified by gas chromatography (Agilent 7890A). The liquid product was detected by a Bruker Avance III 600 MHz system with water suppression. DFT Calculations. All of the first-principles spin-polarized calculations were performed by using the Vienna ab initio simulation program (VASP).51,52 For the exchange−correlation energy of
interacting electrons, the generalized gradient approximation (GGA) with the parametrization of Perdew−Burke−Ernzerhof (PBE) was used.53 To representing the nonvalence core electrons, the projector augmented wave function (PAW) method was used.54 In this work, the MXene functionalized by O atoms is modeled as a monolayer 2D sheet in a supercell consisting of a 3 × 3 unit cell (Ti27C18O18). For Cu particles, we used a 3 × 3 unit cell of Cu(100) surface model. The Cu(100) slab has four atom layers, in which the top two layers of the surfaces together with the adsorbed species were allowed to relax, while the bottom two layers were kept fixed to represent the bulk properties. A vacuum space exceeding 20 Å was employed to avoid the interaction between two periodic units. To ensure our calculation accurate, for all geometry relaxation calculations reported herein, we used a 500 eV cutoff for the kinetic energy of the plane-wave basis set, and a 5 × 5 × 1 Monkhorst−Pack55 k grid was used for sampling the Brillouin zones at structure calculation. The convergence criteria of structure optimization were chosen as the maximum force on each atom less than 0.02 eV Å−1 with an energy change less than 1 × 10−5 eV. The Grimme DFT-D3 scheme of dispersion correction was adopted to describe the van der Waals (vdW) interactions in these layered systems.56
The standard hydrogen electrode model proposed by Nørskov et al. was employed to calculate the Gibbs free energy change (ΔG) for each elemental step.57 The ΔG is defined as
Δ = Δ + Δ − ΔG E T SZPE
where ΔE is the adsorption energy based on density functional theory calculations, ΔZPE is the zero-point energy correction, T is the temperature, and ΔS is the entropy change.
